newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asian Grains - Chinese corn tempts Japan, Korea.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grains - Chinese corn tempts Japan, Korea.

text.p: Japanese trade houses will continue to buy U.S. corn this week, but prices of Chinese and South American-origins are becoming increasingly attractive for buyers in Japan and also South Korea, traders said on Monday.
"China is now offering corn with almost the same price level as the U.S., but we can't confirm any deal so far," a corn trader at a major trade house in Tokyo said.
Talk was circulating in the market that a Tokyo-based trade house is about to reach a corn import deal with China.
Japan has bought more than 80 percent of its April/June U.S. corn requirements, dealers said. U.S. corn premiums were quoted at about 97 U.S. cents a bushel over the CBOT May contract.

South Korean buyers were also seen seeking more Chinese corn for July shipment or later, eschewing U.S. corn to take advantage of lower prices, shorter shipping periods, and smaller cargoes, traders said.
"There is good demand for Chinese corn by local buyers due to more attractive prices and shorter delivery periods," a trader with Cheiljedang Corp said.
Korean feed millers on Monday bought 59,500 tonnes of Chinese corn at between US$139.90-$141.60 a tonne C&F through private negotiations. U.S. corn prices are being quoted at around $152 a tonne C&F.

"Domestic buyers recently have been looking for corn not only for smaller vessels suitable for minor ports but also for Panamax-size vessels for major ports," a trader with a Seoul-based foreign grain trading house said.
"Chinese corn cargoes also enable us to easily manage our feedgrain inventory in factories," the Cheiljedang dealer said.
South Korean buyers bought a total of 111,500 tonnes of Chinese corn at around $141 a tonne C&F last month.
Traders said most South Korean corn buyers have already covered their needs for first half shipment. The South Koreans are buying between 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes of corn a month.
Japanese importers are likewise buying U.S. soybeans for April shipment and premiums were quoted at about 116 U.S. cents a bushel over the CBOT March position.

U.S. Gulf/Japan freight rates eased on Monday, after firming last week. The rate fell to below $26 a tonne for nearby shipment, from about $27 last week. Rates firmed recently on steady demand for vessels to ship steel and coal.
Korean flour millers were also seen probably buying at least 21,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat this week for shipment in April-May to the port of Pusan, traders said.

The Seoul-based foreign grain trading house trader said the freight rate from the U.S. Pacific Northwest was unchanged at between $14.50-$15.00 a tonne. The rate from the U.S. Gulf also remained flat at $24.50-$25.00 a tonne.
In another development, Japanese agricultural cooperative Zen-Noh said its U.S. grain shipments to Japan were proceeding on schedule despite an accident at its loading elevator in Louisiana.
"We originally expected a detailed damage assessment from engineers by last week. But no report is available for some reason at the moment," an official of Zen-Noh in Tokyo said.

Zen-Noh has asked other U.S. grain firms for help in loading grain destined for Japan, he said. The National Federation of Agricultural Co-operative Associations (Zen-Noh) is Japan's largest grain importer.
The Philippines will also probably enter the market to buy more wheat and rice this week to boost its food buffer stocks, traders said.
"Rice and wheat will still be the play next week," a senior trader at one of the Philippines' largest flour millers said.
